transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-04-10
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Sentinel Platform), Marco Silva (ML Infra), J. Kim (Security), Oliver Park (SRE)

[00:00] Ava: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh this is ava from Redwood, i'm the AE, with ravi our se. we planned a deep dive on private vpc networking and some runtime perf stuff. can we quick intro from your side?
[00:10] Lena: yes hi lena here, platform eng, we're evaluating private redwood deployment in our aws org, looking for network patterns and perf numbers for inference at scale.
[00:20] Marco: marco, ml infra, i'll own the benchmarking and infra setup.
[00:25] J. Kim: j. kim security, i'll ask the compliance questions.
[00:30] Ravi: great thanks, so agenda: private link vs vpc peering, nat/egress, subnets & az placement, dns resolution and then runtime items - kv cache, batching, quant, plus next steps.

[05:02] Ava: first up, private link. lena, are you planning to keep control plane in our hosted offering or full private control plane on your VPC?
[05:15] Lena: we want private control plane in our vpc if possible - need traffic to never hit public internet, and we prefer aws managed endpoints.
[05:23] Ravi: ok so we support two main patterns: PrivateLink endpoints to our control plane (we provision a VPC endpoint service) or VPC peering / transit connectivity for full private deployments. PrivateLink gives you per-AZ endpoints and keeps control traffic inside aws fabric, easier on security side. Peering/transit is lower latency for high throughput but requires route table management and cross-account peering.
[06:10] Marco: latency numbers? peering vs privatelink?
[06:20] Ravi: rough guidance: PrivateLink adds a small hop and you may see +2-6ms median depending on AZ topology. VPC peering (or same VPC) is generally lower, sub-ms to low ms, but also depends on nic and eni placement. For GPU hosts doing 8k token contexts, that 2-6ms is noise compared to token generation but for sub-50ms end-to-end requirements it matters.

[12:45] J. Kim: what about NAT and egress IPs - we need static egress IPs for allowlists at partner endpoints.
[12:55] Ravi: two patterns: route egress through NAT Gateways (per-AZ or centralized) or use Egress-only NAT instances with Elastic IPs. NAT Gateway is managed but billable by bytes and hour; costs can grow. For static allowlist we recommend a small fleet of NATs in a dedicated egress subnet with sticky eips or use AWS Global Accelerator for stable IPs. Also you can proxy only non-sensitive parts out; data plane for inference stays private.

[18:30] Ava: any security docs?
[18:33] Marco: (interject) also curious about SGs and ports - what ports does the redwood runtime need for private deploy?
[18:40] Ravi: runtime primarily needs TLS on port 443 for the control plane endpoints. The serving hosts open gRPC ports for internal traffic (4500-ish) between orchestrator and runtime; we'll provide exact ports in the network doc. SGs should allow inbound from your app subnets and from the control-plane endpoint SG. Egress only for updates if you opt-in.

[25:00] Lena: DNS - we run internal split-horizon, does Redwood support custom private dns names?
[25:10] Ravi: yes we recommend privatelink with aws private dns enabled or a Route53 private hosted zone with conditional forwarding. If you want friendly names like runtime.redwood.sentinel.internal we can point to the endpoint ENIs via privatedns. Be careful about resolver order though, some clusters prefer the VPC resolver for internal names.

[30:45] Oliver: what about subnets and AZ placement for gpu hosts - single AZ or multi-AZ?
[30:55] Ravi: for latency-critical inference, place serving hosts in the same AZs as your app frontends to minimize cross-AZ hops. Multi-AZ for resiliency - we recommend deploying at least two AZs with cross-AZ failover. If you want predictable throughput, dedicated capacity pools (we map to a set of instances/hosts in specific subnets) are pinned to specific subnets/AZs. We'll share a recommended subnet CIDR layout.

[38:10] Marco: switching to runtime: kv cache - can you explain cold start behaviour and hit rates?
[38:22] Ravi: sure, KV cache stores cached key/value attention states for repeated prefixes. Cold start means first request must compute and populate cache; subsequent requests with shared prefixes benefit. Hit rate depends on request repetition - we typically see 70-95% effective reduction in token compute for common chat bots with prefix reuse. For very diverse workloads hit rate drops. Also note cache size scales with sequence length and total concurrent contexts; memory on the GPU matters.
[40:10] Marco: how does this interact with batching?
[40:16] Ravi: batching groups tokens across requests, increasing GPU utilization but also introduces added latency while waiting for batch window. If you have high concurrency, batching is great. For low concurrency but predictable latency use smaller batch sizes and KV cache - you still get per-token speedups for cache hits. We provide suggestions in the Optimize tool; for private deploys we can tune batching parameters per-customer.

[45:50] Lena: quantization - do you recommend int8 for production? any accuracy drops?
[45:58] Ravi: quantization gives big memory and throughput wins. int8 or q4_* variants are common. Tradeoff depends on model: some open models have negligible quality loss at int8 for generation, others show regressions in edge cases. We recommend running evals on your prompt sets. For strict quality SLAs, keep fp16 for critical routes and use quant for high-volume lower-criticality routes. We'll share quant profiles and past eval summaries.

[52:30] J. Kim: audit logs and KMS - how are keys managed for private?
[52:36] Ravi: for Redwood Private, you can integrate your KMS/HSM for secrets and model keys. Audit logs stream to your CloudWatch or S3; we can enable S3 server-side encryption with your kms key. Also support for SSO provisioning and RBAC, we'll share SOC2 docs and the compliance pack.

[60:05] Marco: ok technically, what's the best pattern if we want private control plane + minimal egress costs?
[60:12] Ravi: recommended pattern: PrivateLink for control plane, service endpoints for S3 (gateway endpoints) so model artifacts don't egress, NAT only for outbound updates and ops, minimize cross-AZ data movement by colocating frontends and serving hosts, and enable prefix/KV caching to reduce per-token compute and egress to model stores. Also consider VPC endpoints to ECR & S3 and SSM endpoints for instances.

[66:00] Ava: quick recap and next steps - we'll send detailed network diagram and PrivateLink setup doc, ravi will run the KV-cache benchmarks and share numbers, lena will send CIDR ranges and allowlist needs. schedule the on-prem connectivity workshop.
[66:20] Lena: sounds good, thanks.
[66:30] Marco: thanks all.

Action items recap in call (verbatim):
- Ava: share PrivateLink & NAT configuration doc and reference diagram.
- Ravi: run KV-cache benchmark at 8k and 16k contexts and share spreadsheet.
- Lena: provide CIDR ranges, expected egress IPs and security policy constraints.
